preamble: Deaspiration of [kʰ] to plain [k]. The classic case is Grassmann's law in Ancient Greek, a dissimilation in which the first of two aspirates in successive syllables loses its aspiration; it is most visible in reduplicated perfects, where the reduplicating syllable of a χ-initial root surfaces with κ. Independently, Sinhala lost the aspiration contrast altogether, so inherited Indo-Aryan kh became k, and Middle Indo-Aryan shows sporadic Grassmann-like dissimilation (Assamese kandh 'shoulder'). In Sanskrit reduplication kh is also deaspirated, but the reduplicant is additionally palatalized to c, so Sanskrit belongs to a different cell.

examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses its aspiration before the aspirated root-initial χ.
Same deaspiration of the reduplicant; participle κεχηνώς.
Sinhala lost the aspiration contrast in plosives; compare Hindustani khānā, which keeps kh.
The Middle Indo-Aryan kh from the kṣ cluster (Pali khīra) appears as plain k; cognate Dhivehi kiru.
Grassmann-like dissimilation in Middle Indo-Aryan: kh loses aspiration before the following aspirate dh.
